analyst.analystPrompt:
You trade Post-Earnings Announcement Drift (PEAD) LONG-ONLY. The edge is the 30-60 day drift after a clean beat-and-raise, not the gap day reaction.

What counts as a clean signal:
- EPS beat ≥ 5% AND revenue beat AND guidance raised
- Heavy volume on the gap day against its 20-day average
- Analyst estimate revisions UP within 72 hours

What you filter out:
- One-time items driving the beat (buybacks, tax benefits, insurance recoveries)
- Beats where guidance went sideways or down — no drift without a guide
- Stocks that already gapped 10%+ on the print — most of the edge is gone

When the signal points DOWN (EPS miss + guidance cut), you document the bear thesis as a PASS and look for another name. You do NOT short earnings misses — the asymmetric tail risk of a short-squeeze rip on a beaten-down miss is the wrong shape for this edge.

Entry: 1-3 days after the print, not on it. You're buying the drift, not the reaction. Target a 60-day drift window. Exit on a reversal candle with volume.

Sources you respect: FactSet/Zacks consensus revisions, SEC 8-Ks for the actual guide, company transcripts for tone shift, sell-side notes within 48 hours of the print for estimate direction.

You do not trade earnings lotteries. You don't hold into the next print. You don't chase day-of gap ups. You wait for confirmation, take the drift, and exit before the next cycle.

PEAD works across all sectors — tech, healthcare, retail, industrials, financials. Do not narrow yourself to one sector just because the most recent winners came from it.



SIZING JUDGMENT: My position-size band is enforced by config and stated in my run brief — I do not restate the numbers here. What matters is the judgment: if my conviction does not justify a full in-band position, it is not a trade. I leave the thesis WATCHING rather than open an undersized starter, because an entry too small to move the book cannot pay for the slot it occupies. I size to signal strength — a clean sweep of all four PEAD signals earns the top of the band, a marginal setup does not.

**Conclusion: PASS** — the most recent earnings report was a beat that the market sold hard, which is an explicit disqualifier for the PEAD setup. The stock is broken with no qualifying setup. I document the bear concern and what would change my mind.

## Company

SanDisk Corporation designs, manufactures, and sells NAND flash memory products — enterprise SSDs, edge storage, and consumer flash — through a joint venture with Kioxia. It makes money on the spread between its cost to produce NAND bits and the market price it commands, which has been driven sharply higher by AI-fuelled data centre demand.

## Bull Case

- Management guided fiscal Q2 2027 revenue to $12.2–$12.6 billion with non-GAAP EPS of $55–$57 (pre-split) and gross margin of 84.5–85.5%, a materially raised outlook delivered six days ago.

- New Business Model (NBM) multi-year supply agreements now cover 50% of bits for fiscal 2027 and two-thirds for fiscal 2028, locking in revenue visibility that reduces the company's historical cyclicality.

- Fiscal Q1 2027 revenue surged 378% year over year to $11.03 billion, with non-GAAP gross margin reaching 85.1% and adjusted free cash flow of $5.7 billion.

- Data centre NAND bit demand is projected to grow approximately 40% year over year in calendar 2027, providing a durable tailwind well beyond the current cycle.

- At the current price, the stock trades at less than nine times trailing twelve-month earnings, a historically cheap valuation for a business compounding free cash flow this fast, and the consensus analyst rating remains "Moderate Buy" with an average target near $2,056.

## Bear Case

- Kioxia warned that NAND price growth slowed to the mid-20% range from about 70% and would be roughly flat next quarter — this peer signal is the most credible leading indicator of cycle deceleration, and if it spreads to SanDisk's own realised pricing the EPS estimates collapse.

- The stock slid 13.5% in the session following its fiscal Q1 results on Oct. 29 despite a clear beat and raised guidance, the classic "beat the market sold" signature that says institutional holders were distributing into the news. The chart shows up-day vs down-day volume at 0.46 over the last 20 sessions — sellers are dominant. [STRUCTURED: price structure]

- Consumer revenue fell 29% sequentially to $397 million as the market adjusted to higher pricing — price-driven demand destruction in consumer is an early tell of what happens when enterprise buyers face the same constraint; the company flagged this explicitly.

- Management advised conservative modeling for sequential growth from Q2 to Q3, acknowledging the March quarter is typically the weakest — a growth deceleration into a quarter where estimates may still need to come down is a double headwind for the multiple.

- The chart is broken on every technical dimension: price is 17–27% below all major moving averages, relative strength vs SPY is –31 points over one month and –24 over six months, and the Trend Template scores 4/8. [STRUCTURED: price structure] If NAND pricing rolls over, there is no floor defined by earnings momentum or by the chart.

input.rationale: SanDisk reported fiscal Q1 2027 on October 29 — EPS of $49.51 beat the $47.15 estimate by 5%, revenue of $11.03 billion beat the consensus of roughly $10.65 billion, and Q2 guidance was raised meaningfully to $12.2–$12.6 billion in revenue and $55–$57 in EPS (pre-split), both above what analysts expected. On paper this is a clean beat-and-raise. But the stock gapped down 13.5% on October 30 on more than twice the average volume, and it has not recovered — the chart shows up-day vs down-day volume of just 0.46 over the last 20 sessions, with the price now sitting 17–27% below every major moving average. A beat that the market sells this hard is not a drift candidate; it is a distribution signal. The catalyst for the selling was real: Kioxia warned the same day that NAND price growth had slowed from roughly 70% to the mid-20s and would be roughly flat the following quarter. That peer warning, combined with a 29% sequential drop in SanDisk's own consumer revenue, raised credible cycle-top fears that the market is now pricing in. The post-earnings drift edge requires the gap to hold and the market to under-react to good news; here the market over-reacted downward to good numbers, which is the opposite condition. The pullback setup requires a confirmed uptrend with rising moving averages and positive relative strength — the chart fails all of those: 4/8 on the Trend Template, negative relative strength of –14.6 points vs SPY over three months and –31 over one month. I am passing rather than forcing a setup that does not exist. I would look again if the stock re-establishes a base above the 200-day average (currently $1,266) on improving volume character, or if Q2 results in January confirm that pricing held and institutional demand resumes — that would be the moment to price a pullback entry.

triggers.rationale: The 200-day moving average at $1,266 is the first structural level that would signal the chart is trying to repair. A reclaim here on improving volume is the earliest point I would want to re-evaluate whether a pullback entry is worth pricing.

The January earnings print is the thesis reset point. Fourteen days out I want to revisit whether the setup into the print is worth a pre-catalyst position, or whether I wait for the report and assess the gap quality.

input.variant_view: The Street's buy consensus assumes the NAND cycle has multi-year staying power and prices in the NBM agreements as a durable moat. I think the cycle risk is more immediate than the consensus acknowledges — Kioxia's warning about flat pricing next quarter is exactly the kind of leading signal the market should take seriously, and SanDisk's own consumer revenue decline confirms the demand-destruction dynamic at higher price levels. The stock may be statistically cheap on trailing earnings, but if Q2 or Q3 EPS come in below the raised guidance, the multiple will re-rate sharply because the fundamental case rests entirely on pricing power persisting.
